note: Typical mistakes are tendencies, not rules about people. They happen because your first language has different sounds, letters or rules: this is called transfer (or interference). Not everyone makes these mistakes, and many learners stop making them quite quickly. If you know where a mistake comes from, you get rid of it faster. Based on comparing the language systems (contrastive linguistics) and on experience from language teaching.

languages.name: English
strengths: English and French share thousands of words from Latin and Old French: important, table, restaurant, université.
English has the sh of “shop” and the s of “measure”, so ch and j are not new to you.

mistakes.wrong: rue, merci said with an English r (tongue curled back)
mistakes.right: rue, merci: r at the back of the mouth
mistakes.why: English r is made with the tongue tip pulled back and round lips. French r is made at the back of the mouth, with friction, and the tongue tip stays down.
English has no sound like the French u. Learners say “oo”, and that is another word: tu / tout, rue / roue.

mistakes.right: bon, vent, vin: a nasal vowel, no n or g
mistakes.why: English has no nasal vowels, so the n or m gets said. In French the vowel itself is nasal, and the n is only a sign.

mistakes.wrong: “ay-tay” for été, “oh-oo” for o, a weak “uh” at the end
mistakes.right: été, mot: one clean vowel in every syllable
mistakes.why: English é and o glide into “ay” and “ow”, and weak syllables turn into “uh”. French vowels stay in one place, in every syllable.
At the start of a word, English p, t, k come with a puff of air. French p, t, k have none, so the puff sounds English at once.

mistakes.right: chocolat, université: even syllables, a little longer at the end
mistakes.why: English stresses one syllable inside each word. French stresses the end of a group, so every syllable counts about the same.

mistakes.wrong: petit, grand, beaucoup with the last letter said
mistakes.right: petit, grand, beaucoup: nothing at the end
mistakes.why: English spelling also hides letters, but you tend to say every French letter you see. Many final consonants are silent: t, d, s, x, p, z. Say them only before a vowel (liaison).

mistakes.wrong: l'hôtel, l'homme with a breath at the h
mistakes.why: English h is a breath. French h is silent: begin on the vowel.
English says I am 25. French says I have 25 years: j'ai 25 ans. The same goes for j'ai chaud, j'ai faim, j'ai peur.
English nouns have no gender. In French every noun is masculine or feminine, and the article, the adjective and the pronoun must agree. Learn each noun with le or la.
Most adjectives follow the noun in French. A small group goes before it (beau, petit, grand, bon, jeune, vieux, nouveau, joli).
English adjectives never change. French adjectives agree with the noun or pronoun: petit, petite, petits, petites.
English uses have for every past tense. French uses être with aller, venir, partir, arriver, sortir and with reflexive verbs: je suis allé, elle s'est levée.

mistakes.right: Je mange une pomme. / Je suis en train de manger une pomme.
mistakes.why: French has no -ing form after être. The present covers both I eat and I am eating. Use être en train de to stress that it is happening right now.
English puts the object after the verb (I saw him). French puts a pronoun before the verb: je le vois, je l'ai vu, je lui parle.
French negation has two parts around the verb: ne … pas. In speech ne is often dropped (je sais pas), but write it.
English uses for, and the present perfect (I have lived here for three years). French uses the present tense with depuis.

mistakes.wrong: J'aime chocolat. Je suis un étudiant.
mistakes.right: J'aime le chocolat. Je suis étudiant.
mistakes.why: French needs an article with a general noun (j'aime le chocolat). With a job, status or nationality after être there is none: je suis étudiant, elle est médecin.
French writes days, months and languages with a small letter. A person from a country has a capital: un Français.
An accent is part of the spelling in French, and it can change the word: a (has) / à (to), ou (or) / où (where). Don't skip accents.
French puts a space before ? ! : and ; (a non-breaking one, if your keyboard allows it). English does not. In texts to friends nobody checks, but in a formal letter it shows.

mistakes.wrong: Je aime le ami de Marc.
mistakes.why: Before a vowel or a silent h, je, le, la, ne, de, me, te, se, que become j', l', n', d', m', t', s', qu'. In English there is nothing like it.
Spelling that differs from English: adresse (one d), comité, appartement (two p). Check the double consonants of words that look English.

mistakes.wrong: Je suis très excité de te voir.
mistakes.right: Je suis très content de te voir.
mistakes.why: French excité means aroused or overexcited, not looking forward to something. Use content, ravi, enthousiaste or j'ai hâte de.

mistakes.wrong: Je joue le tennis. Je joue la guitare.
mistakes.right: Je joue au tennis. Je joue de la guitare.
mistakes.why: English plays everything. French uses jouer à for sports and games, and jouer de for instruments.

mistakes.right: Je voudrais un café, s'il vous plaît.
mistakes.why: Je veux (I want) is a demand. Je voudrais (I would like) is the polite form for shops, restaurants and offices.

languages.name: German
strengths: German has ü and ö, so the French u and eu are not new to you.
German has the sh sound (Schule), and its h and r are close to the sounds you need.

mistakes.right: bon, vent, vin: a nasal vowel, no n or g
mistakes.why: German only has nasal vowels in loan words (Teint, Chanson). Usually the n gets said, or becomes “ng”. In French the vowel is nasal, and nothing follows it.

mistakes.wrong: il a said with a small stop before a: “il | a”
mistakes.right: il a = “i-la”: the l moves on
mistakes.why: German starts a vowel with a glottal stop (Knacklaut: “der | Apfel”). French doesn't: it joins words, and the consonant moves on to the next vowel.

mistakes.right: zéro: a voiced z, as in German Sonne
mistakes.why: German z is ts. French z is the voiced s of Sonne, which is also the s of maison. Between vowels one s is z, two ss is s: poison and poisson differ.

mistakes.right: robe, rouge, bague: the voice stays on to the end
mistakes.why: German makes final voiced consonants voiceless (Rad = Rat). French keeps them voiced: bague is not bac, code is not cote.

mistakes.wrong: les amis said “les | amis” with a pause, or with a sharp s
mistakes.right: les amis = lé-z-ami: the s sounds like z
mistakes.why: German has no liaison: words stay apart. In French the final s, x becomes z, and d becomes t, and the sound joins the next word.

mistakes.wrong: petit, grand, trop with the last letter said (“petit-t”)
mistakes.right: petit, grand, trop: nothing at the end
mistakes.why: German says the letters it sees, so “Paris” gets its s. Many final consonants are silent in French; the feminine form shows them: petit / petite.

mistakes.wrong: table, Suisse said “ta-ble-e” with a German weak -e
mistakes.right: table = “tabl”: no vowel at the end
mistakes.why: German ends many words in a weak e (Tasse). In French a final e is silent, and the word ends on the consonant before it.

mistakes.wrong: hôtel, homme with a breath at the start
mistakes.why: German h is said at the start of a word (Haus). French h is silent.
German has der Mond (m) and die Sonne (f). In French it is the other way round: le soleil, la lune. Gender is not the same in the two languages: learn it with the noun.
German predicate adjectives don't change (sie ist klein). In French they agree with the subject: elle est petite, ils sont petits.
German says ich bin 25 (Jahre alt). French says I have 25 years: j'ai 25 ans.
German kein becomes pas de in French: je n'ai pas de frère, il n'y a pas de pain. After a negation un, une, du, des turn into de or d'.

mistakes.wrong: Quand j'ai été petit, j'ai joué dehors.
mistakes.right: Quand j'étais petit, je jouais dehors.
mistakes.why: German speakers use the Perfekt for most past events. In French the passé composé is for events (hier, j'ai joué), the imparfait for habits and descriptions in the past (quand j'étais petit, je jouais).
German says ich wasche mir die Hände with a dative pronoun. French says je me lave les mains: the reflexive pronoun, then the article. No possessive.
German zum Arzt, French chez le médecin: you go to a person's place with chez (chez le dentiste, chez moi), to a place with à.
German sich interessieren für, French s'intéresser à. Verbs often take different prepositions: learn them with the verb.
German says Klavier spielen without an article. French needs jouer de for instruments: du piano, de la guitare. Sports and games take à: au foot.

mistakes.wrong: Le Livre est sur la Table.
mistakes.right: Le livre est sur la table.
mistakes.why: German writes every noun with a capital. French only writes names, places and the first word of a sentence with a capital.

mistakes.wrong: Je pense, que tu as raison.
mistakes.right: Je pense que tu as raison.
mistakes.why: German puts a comma before every subordinate clause. French has no comma before que, parce que and si.
German bekommen looks like devenir (become), but means recevoir (get). Devenir is only to become: il devient médecin.
German kennen is connaître (people, places). German wissen and können are savoir. Skills: je sais nager, je sais conduire.
German also (so, well) is alors or donc in French. French aussi means also, too: moi aussi.
A French gymnase is a sports hall. The school that German Gymnasium looks like is the lycée (and the collège before it).

languages.name: Spanish
strengths: Spanish and French share a lot of Latin vocabulary: familia, importante, restaurante.
Spanish vowels are clean and short, and Spanish has no weak “uh”, which helps for a, i, o.

mistakes.wrong: tu, rue said “tu”, “rue” as in Spanish
mistakes.right: tu, rue: “ee” with round lips; tout: ou
mistakes.why: Spanish has only one u, and it is French ou. French has two: tout / tu. Say tu with your tongue forward, and it won't be a different word.

mistakes.right: deux, peur: eu, round lips and the tongue of é
mistakes.why: Spanish has no rounded front vowels. The nearest sound is ou or o, but deux is not doux, and peur is not pour.

mistakes.wrong: pan, bon said “pan”, “bon” with a full n, as in Spanish
mistakes.right: pain, bon: nasal vowel, no n
mistakes.why: Spanish says every n. In French an n or m after a vowel (at the end or before a consonant) gives a nasal vowel, and isn't said.

mistakes.wrong: poison, maison, rose said with an s (“poi-son”), zéro with s or th
mistakes.right: poison, maison, rose: a z between vowels
mistakes.why: In standard Spanish the s is always s, and there is no z. In French s between vowels is z: poison is not poisson.

mistakes.right: vin, vous: top teeth on the lip, voice on
mistakes.why: Spanish b and v are one sound. French has two: b with both lips, v with your teeth on the lip. vin is not bain.

mistakes.wrong: jour, jaune said “khour” or “dyour”, chat said “tchat”
mistakes.right: jour: voiced like the s in “measure”; chat: sh
mistakes.why: Spanish ch is the ch of “church” and j is a rasp. French ch is sh, and j is the voiced sh, with no t or d before it.

mistakes.wrong: demain, table said “de-main”, “ta-ble” with a full e
mistakes.why: Spanish gives every vowel its full sound. In French an unstressed e is weak, and a final e is silent.

mistakes.wrong: petit, grand, trop said with the last letter (“petit-t”)
mistakes.right: petit, grand, trop: nothing at the end
mistakes.why: Spanish writes what it says. Many French final consonants are silent: t, d, s, x, p, z. Learn them with the feminine: petit / petite.
Several nouns have the other gender in Spanish: la leche → le lait, el mar → la mer, la sangre → le sang, la miel → le miel. Check the gender of every word you think you know.

mistakes.right: Je parle français. Je suis fatigué.
mistakes.why: Spanish drops the subject pronoun (hablo, estoy). French can't: je, tu, il, elle, on, nous, vous, ils, elles are required before the verb.
Spanish puts a before a person object (vi a Paul). French has no such preposition: j'ai vu Paul, j'aime Marie.
Spanish no is one word. French negation needs two: ne … pas. Ne goes before the verb, pas after.
Spanish pensar en, French penser à. Many prepositions differ: learn them with the verb (penser à, rêver de, compter sur).

mistakes.wrong: Il a beaucoup de gens ici.
mistakes.right: Il y a beaucoup de gens ici.
mistakes.why: Spanish hay is il y a in French. Not il a (he has): il y a une pharmacie près d'ici.

mistakes.right: Je dois partir. / Il faut que je parte.
mistakes.why: Spanish tengo que irme is not j'ai que partir. French uses devoir + infinitive or il faut que + subjunctive.
Spanish hacer una pregunta, French poser une question. You can ask, put or pose a question, but not make one.
French has no opening ¿ or ¡. A question mark or an exclamation mark only comes at the end, with a space before it (Comment vas-tu ?).
Spanish ñ is gn in French (montagne, campagne). Spanish -ción is -tion (la nation, l'information).
Check doubles and accents of words that look Spanish: appartement, immédiatement, commun, adresse.

mistakes.wrong: Je suis constipée : j'ai le nez qui coule.
mistakes.right: Je suis enrhumée : j'ai le nez qui coule.
mistakes.why: Spanish constipado means having a cold. French constipé is a digestion problem. A cold is un rhume: je suis enrhumé.
Spanish salir is sortir in French. French salir means to make dirty: tu vas salir tes chaussures.

mistakes.wrong: Le film est large : il dure trois heures.
mistakes.right: Le film est long : il dure trois heures.
mistakes.why: Spanish largo (long) is long in French. French large means wide: une rue large.

languages.name: Portuguese
strengths: Portuguese has nasal vowels and the sounds sh and zh (chave, já), so more of the French inventory is familiar to you than to most learners.
Many Portuguese words are close to French ones: possível/possible, importante, restaurante.

mistakes.wrong: tu, rue said “tu”, “rua” as in Portuguese
mistakes.why: Portuguese u is the French ou. French has two sounds: tu and tout. Say tu with a forward tongue.

mistakes.right: deux, peur: eu, round lips and the tongue of é
mistakes.why: Portuguese has no rounded front vowels, so eu turns into ou or o. deux is not doux.

mistakes.wrong: vin, bon said like Portuguese “vĩ”, “bõ”, with a closed vowel and a nasal glide
mistakes.right: vin: open ɛ̃, bon: open ɔ̃, with no glide
mistakes.why: Portuguese speakers know nasal vowels, which helps. But the French ones are more open (vin sounds a bit like “vain”, bon like “bawn”) and stop with no nasal glide or consonant.

mistakes.wrong: rue, merci said with a rolled r (European Portuguese) or a breathy h (Brazil)
mistakes.right: rue: voiced friction at the back, no roll
mistakes.why: Many Portuguese r sounds are close to the French r. A rolled r must move to the back of the mouth, and an h-like r needs voice.
Brazilian Portuguese adds a small i after a final consonant, and often says every e. In French a final e is silent and the word ends on its consonant.
Some nouns have the other gender in Portuguese: a viagem → le voyage, o sangue → le sang. Check the gender of every word you think you know.
Portuguese often leaves out the subject (moro em Lyon). French needs the pronoun every time: j'habite, tu habites, il habite.

mistakes.wrong: J'aime de la musique. J'aime de danser.
mistakes.why: Portuguese gostar de needs de. French aimer is followed directly by the noun or the infinitive.

mistakes.wrong: Il a beaucoup de gens dans la rue.
mistakes.right: Il y a beaucoup de gens dans la rue.
mistakes.why: Portuguese tem (in Brazil) and há are il y a in French. Il a means he has.
Portuguese says o meu livro with an article. French has no article before mon, ton, son, notre, votre, leur.

mistakes.right: Je fais mes devoirs. / Je suis en train de faire mes devoirs.
mistakes.why: Brazilian estou fazendo has no -ant form after être in French. Use the present, or être en train de + infinitive.
Portuguese não is one word. French negation has two parts: ne … pas.
Portuguese -ção is -tion in French (nação → la nation), and not -ssion or -çion. Double the m or the n where French does: communication.

mistakes.wrong: J'assiste un film à la télé.
mistakes.right: Je regarde un film à la télé.
mistakes.why: Portuguese assistir (a um filme) is regarder. French assister à means to be present at an event: j'assiste à une réunion.

mistakes.wrong: J'espère le bus depuis dix minutes.
mistakes.right: J'attends le bus depuis dix minutes.
mistakes.why: Portuguese esperar means to wait and to hope. In French espérer is to hope, and attendre is to wait.
In Portugal constipado is having a cold. French constipé is a digestion problem. A cold is un rhume.

mistakes.wrong: Je fais une question à la professeure.
mistakes.right: Je pose une question à la professeure.
mistakes.why: Portuguese fazer uma pergunta, French poser une question.

languages.name: Italian
strengths: Italian has gn (gnocchi) and sh (scena), and shares most of its vocabulary with French.
Italian vowels are clean and short, as French vowels should be.

mistakes.wrong: pomme, belle, année said with a long double consonant
mistakes.right: pomme, belle, année: one short consonant
mistakes.why: Italian holds its double consonants. In French a double letter is only spelling: say a single consonant.

mistakes.wrong: tu, rue said “tu”, “rue” as in Italian
mistakes.why: Italian u is the French ou. French also has a second u: tu is not tout.

mistakes.right: deux, peur: eu, round lips and the tongue of é
mistakes.why: Italian has no rounded front vowels, so eu turns into o or ou.

mistakes.wrong: bon, vin said “bon-n”, “vin-n” with a clear n
mistakes.right: bon, vin: nasal vowel, no n
mistakes.why: Italian says every n. In French the n or m after a vowel is only a sign of the nasal vowel.

mistakes.right: ordinateur, important: even, a little longer at the end
mistakes.why: Italian words have a strong syllable inside the word. In French only the end of a group is stressed, so every syllable counts about the same.

mistakes.wrong: table, rouge said “tabl-e”, “rou-ge” with a final vowel
mistakes.why: Italian words end in a clear vowel. A French final e is silent; the word ends on the consonant before it.
Some nouns have the other gender in Italian: il fiore → la fleur, il dente → la dent. Check the gender of every word you think you know.

mistakes.right: Je mange du pain. J'ai des amis.
mistakes.why: Italian says mangio pane, ho amici. French needs du, de la, des: je mange du pain, j'ai des amis.
Italian ne is en in French: ne ho tre → j'en ai trois. The pronoun en is required when you leave the noun out after a number or a quantity.
Italian dal medico is chez le médecin in French. Not du (a form of de), and not au. Chez is for a person's place.

mistakes.right: J'aime le café. / Le café me plaît.
mistakes.why: Italian mi piace il caffè is built with the thing as the subject. French also has plaire, but aimer is easier: j'aime le café.
Italian non voglio niente is a negation with niente. In French ne … rien has no pas: je ne veux rien, je ne vois personne.
Italian polite Lei uses the third person. French uses vous (second person plural): vous parlez, vous êtes.
Italian f is ph in many French words of Greek origin: photo, téléphone, philosophie, pharmacie.
Italian e is et in French. The word est (is) sounds the same: Paul est là.

mistakes.wrong: J'ai réservé une camera à l'hôtel.
mistakes.right: J'ai réservé une chambre à l'hôtel.
mistakes.why: Italian camera is a room. French caméra is a film camera. A room is une chambre.

mistakes.wrong: Le bus ne ferme pas ici.
mistakes.right: Le bus ne s'arrête pas ici.
mistakes.why: Italian fermare is to stop. French fermer is to close: fermer la porte, fermer un compte.

mistakes.wrong: Tous mes parents viennent au mariage : oncles et cousins.
mistakes.right: Toute ma famille vient au mariage : oncles et cousins.
mistakes.why: Italian parenti means relatives. French les parents are mother and father.

mistakes.wrong: Je fais une question au professeur.
mistakes.right: Je pose une question au professeur.
mistakes.why: Italian fare una domanda is poser une question in French.

languages.name: Arabic
strengths: Many Arabic speakers know French from school, family or the Maghreb, and the guttural sounds of Arabic (غ, خ) make the French r easier than for most learners.
Arabic already has gender, agreement of adjectives and a rich verb system, so these ideas are not new.

mistakes.right: pain, pas: a p without voice
mistakes.why: Standard Arabic has no p, only b. Close your lips and stay voiceless: a quiet throat for p, a buzz for b.
Arabic has no u like the French one. Say “ee”, then round the lips, and tu isn't tout.

mistakes.right: deux, peur: eu, round lips and the tongue of é
mistakes.why: Arabic has no rounded front vowels. Say é, then round your lips: that is eu.

mistakes.wrong: bon, vin said “bonn”, “vinn” with a clear n
mistakes.right: bon, vin: nasal vowel, no n
mistakes.why: Arabic has no nasal vowels, so the n gets said. In French the vowel is nasal, and the n is a sign.
Arabic script has no capital letters, so a name looks the same at the start and in the middle. In French, names, cities and the first word of a sentence start with a capital. Days and months don't.
Arabic has no p, so p can come out as b in writing as in speech: pomme, pain, pharmacie, plat. Check words with p.
Arabic has no verb for to be in the present (ana talib). French needs it: je suis, tu es, il est.
Arabic has no word for a. In French you need an article before a noun: un, une, des. The exceptions are after a job: je suis professeur.
Arabic adjectives follow the noun. French adjectives usually do too (une voiture rouge), but some very common ones go before: beau, joli, petit, grand, bon, jeune, vieux, nouveau.
Arabic joins two nouns directly (sayyarat Paul). French needs de: la voiture de Paul, la maison de mes parents.
Arabic relative clauses repeat the noun as a pronoun (al-rajul alladhi ra'aytuhu). French has que, which already stands for the object: l'homme que j'ai vu.

quiz.prompt: Why do many learners with Arabic as their first language write names with a small letter?
options: Their script has no capital letters
In Arabic everything is written in capitals
quiz.answer: Their script has no capital letters
quiz.explain: In French, names, cities and the first word of a sentence start with a capital letter.

quiz.prompt: How do you say your age correctly?
quiz.explain: French uses avoir for age: j'ai 25 ans. English and German use to be.
You borrow in a bibliothèque and buy in a librairie.

quiz.prompt: You moved here three years ago and you still live here. What is correct?
options: J'ai habité ici depuis trois ans.
quiz.explain: Present tense + depuis for something that started in the past and still goes on.

quiz.prompt: You like books. What do you say?
quiz.explain: Aimer takes the thing directly and needs the article for a general noun.

quiz.prompt: Where does the adjective usually go in French?
options: Usually after the noun, but a few common ones go before
quiz.answer: Usually after the noun, but a few common ones go before
quiz.explain: Une voiture rouge, but une belle maison, un petit appartement.

quiz.prompt: What is the difference between a and à?
options: a is the verb avoir, à is a preposition
à is the plural of a
quiz.answer: a is the verb avoir, à is a preposition
quiz.explain: Il a faim (he has hunger), il va à Paris (he goes to Paris). Replace a with avait to test it.

quiz.prompt: You feel cold. What do you say?
quiz.explain: Feelings of the body use avoir: j'ai froid, j'ai chaud, j'ai faim, j'ai soif.

quiz.prompt: What is un gymnase in France?
quiz.explain: The school is le lycée. A gymnase is the hall where sport is taught.
